questions.question: Which of the following conditions is associated with a right shift in Arneth count?

explanation.text: The presence of older neutrophils (N4 and N5) indicates suppression of bone marrow with a shift to the right in Arneth count. The Arneth count is a method used to classify neutrophils as N1 to N5 based on the number of lobes in their nuclei.

Classification of Neutrophil Class I: Myelocytes and neutrophils with indented or horseshoe-shaped nuclei. (5%) Class II: Neutrophils with bilobed nuclei. (35%) Class III: Neutrophils with tri-lobed nuclei. (41%) Class IV: Neutrophils with four-lobed nuclei. (17%) Class V: Neutrophils with five or more lobes in their nuclei. (2%) Toxic Conditions Fewer cells in Classes IV and V indicate a left-sided shift Active tuberculosis often shows a left shift. (Option A) Other infections showing a left shift may have superimposed tuberculosis Extrinsic Factors Influencing Arneth Count Certain drugs, tissue extracts, and hormones.

Trauma, various forms of radiation. Induction of anesthesia. Infections and Arneth Count Acute progressive infections: Notable left shift. (Option B) As infection subsides: Less marked left shift, may shift to the right. Chronic infections: Other features like lymphocytosis come into range. Normal Neutrophil Distribution N1 and N3 constitute most neutrophils in peripheral blood.

Bone Marrow Stimulation Presence of younger neutrophils (N1 and N2) indicates stimulation of bone marrow (shift to the left). (Option D) Bone Marrow Suppression Presence of older cells (N4 and N5) indicates suppression of bone marrow (shift to right) (Option C) Hypersegmented Neutrophil Seen in megaloblastic anemia due to folate and vitamin B12 deficiency (shift to right)

questions.question: Which of the following statements about platelets are true?

options.A: Alpha granules contain clotting factors and platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF)
options.B: Splenectomy causes a decrease in the platelet count
options.C: Interleukins IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, and IL-7 are involved in stimulating platelet production
options.D: Thrombopoietin is produced exclusively by megakaryocytes and regulates platelet production

explanation.text: Alpha granules are abundant in platelets, about 50-80 granules per platelet. They contain secreted proteins like clotting factors and platelet-derived growth factor(PDGF).

Platelets General Description Small, granulated, non-nucleated discs important for hemostasis Size 1-4 µm in diameter Concentration in Blood 150,000 - 450,000/µL Half-life ~4 days Origin Formed from megakaryocytes in the bone marrow Distribution 60-75% in circulation; the remainder mainly in the spleen Splenectomy Effect Causes an increase in platelet count (thrombocytosis) (Option B) Thrombopoietin Produced by liver and kidneys; regulates platelet production (Option D) Membrane Receptors For collagen, ADP, von Willebrand factor and fibrinogen Cytoplasmic Components Actin, myosin, glycogen, lysosomes and granules Granules Alpha granules: Soluble coagulation proteins (vWF, Factor V, II), adhesion molecule, growth factor (IGF, PDGF, TGF-β, platelet factor 4), Integrin, Cytokines (Option A) Dense granules: ADP, ATP, Calcium, Serotonin Response to Injury Adhere to exposed collagen and von Willebrand factor; release granule contents upon activation Deficiency Effect Thrombocytopenic purpura (easy bruising, multiple subcutaneous hemorrhages) Interleukins IL-1, IL-3, IL-6, IL-11 stimulate platelet production (Option C) Factors increasing platelet synthesis Inflammation, thrombopoietin and IL-1, IL-3, IL-6,
IL-11

questions.question: A 45-year-old patient needs an urgent blood transfusion. The image below shows the results of the patient’s blood group typing test. Based on the agglutination patterns observed, identify the patient's blood group?

explanation.text: In the above clinical scenario, the image shows agglutination with anti-A and anti-B and positive anti-D (Rh) sera, indicating the presence of A antigen, B antigen and positive Rh factor. Therefore, the blood group is AB positive (AB+ve).

A-B-O System: Blood type Antigens on RBC Antibodies in Plasma Genotypes Frequency O - Anti-A and Anti-B OO 47% A A Anti-B OA or AA 41% B B Anti-A OB or BB 9% AB A and B - AB 3% Landsteiner's Law states that if a particular agglutinogen is present on the red cell membrane of an individual, the corresponding agglutinin must be absent in his plasma and vice versa.

Agglutination test results: H Antigen: The H gene codes for fucose transferase, forming the H antigen, found in all blood types. In addition, Type A adds N-acetylgalactosamine, Type B adds galactose, Type AB has both transferases, and Type O has neither, leaving the H antigen unchanged. Blood group O with H antigen in plasma or saliva is called the OH group or Bombay (Oh: if H is not dominant).

Bombay Blood Group: Phenotype: Oh, lacking the H gene and unable to form A or B antigens. Identified as group O in routine tests, with serum containing anti-A, anti-B, and anti-H antibodies. Therefore transfusion can be done only with Bombay blood group.

Rh Factor: Common Rh antigens C, D, E, c, d and e Detection Only in red cells D antigen Most antigenic, defines Rh positive No D antigen Rh negative; Forms anti-D agglutinins upon exposure to Rh+ cells (Option B) Prevalence 85% of whites Rh+ve,15% Rh-ve Over 99% of Asians Rh+ve Anti-D antibody formation Requires exposure (transfusion or
feto-maternal blood transfer) to D-positive red cells Transfusion reaction onset Requires massive exposure to Rh antigen to produce enough agglutinins for significant transfusion reaction to develop

questions.question: A pediatrician is reviewing the development of hematopoiesis in a fetus at various stages of gestation. They are particularly interested in understanding the shifts in hematopoietic activity locations as the fetus develops. At which gestational age does the bone marrow become the primary site of hematopoiesis?

explanation.text: At birth, hemopoiesis stops in liver and gets confined only to the bone marrow. Thus bone marrow becomes the primary site for hematopoiesis at birth. When hemopoiesis occurs in liver and spleen in postnatal life, is called extramedullary hemopoiesis. Stage Location Key Points Mesoblastic Yolk sac, PSP, AGM Yolk sac: Multilineage differentiating capabilities (starts functioning by the 2nd week of gestation).

Non-yolk sac regions: Para Aortic splanchnopleura (PSP) and aorta-gonad mesonephros (AGM) regions. PSP: Gives rise to B-cell progenitors. AGM: Contains pluripotent stem cells. Hepatic Liver, spleen 2nd trimester of pregnancy. Liver: Hematopoiesis starts at the 5th week, peaks at the 5th month, and ceases at birth. Spleen: Hematopoiesis mainly in the 2nd trimester, less than liver.

Postnatal: Normally does not occur in liver and spleen unless demand is high (extramedullary hemopoiesis). Medullary Bone marrow (medullary hemopoiesis). Marrow cavities appear by the 5th month (around 20 weeks) of fetal life, and become hemopoietic. (Option C) Initial phase: Bone marrow exclusive for granulocytic and megakaryocytic proliferation.

Erythropoiesis starts in bone marrow towards the end of the 3rd trimester, and continues throughout life. Postnatal: Hemopoiesis confined to bone marrow, extramedullary hemopoiesis abnormal. Option A: At 3 to 6 weeks, hematopoiesis occur in yolk sac which starts functioning from 2 weeks of gestational age known as Mesoblastic stage.

Option B: At 6 to 8 weeks, hematopoiesis occur in liver which starts functioning from 5 weeks of gestational age, peaks at 5th month and ceases at birth, known as Hepatic stage. Option C: Around 20 week s: Hematopoiesis starts to occur in the bone marrow around 20 weeks but liver becomes the major site of hematopoiesis.

questions.question: A researcher is studying the behavior of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and wants to understand the mechanisms that regulate their self-renewal during tissue repair. Which type of stem cell division increases the stem cell pool during tissue repair?

explanation.text: Symmetric division results in both daughter cells retaining stem cell properties, thereby increasing the stem cell pool, which is crucial during tissue repair.

Pathway Definition Mechanisms / Factors Signaling Pathways Self-Renewal Produces at least one daughter cell with stem cell properties Symmetric and Asymmetric Division Wnt, Notch, TGF-β Differentiation Produces specialized cell types Transcription Factors, Microenvironmental Signals Wnt, Notch, TGF-β Both Pathways Balance between self-renewal and differentiation to maintain stem cell pool and tissue function Interplay of intrinsic and extrinsic factors Stem cell types and their properties: Stem Cell Type Description Example Totipotent Stem Cells Can generate the entire organism, including the placenta.

Single cell from the 8-cell embryo stage. Pluripotent Stem Cells Can generate the entire organism except the placenta. Cells from the inner cell mass of the blastocyst. Multipotent Stem Cells Can form only one lineage of cells. Hematopoietic stem cells that give rise to various blood cell types.

Steps in hematopoiesis: Multipotent Stem Cell → Progenitor Cell → Precursor Cell → Mature Cell Mature Cell: Differentiated cell with decreased self-renewal and proliferation properties. Hematopoietic Stem Cells: Convert to multipotent stem cells, giving rise to two progenitor types. Memory B and T Cells are mature cells but have the ability to self-renew and proliferate.
**Asymmetric division (Option A):** Maintains homeostasis by generating one stem cell and one differentiated cell, rather than expanding the pool.

**Terminal differentiation (Option C):** Leads to fully specialized cells with no further division Lateral inhibition (Option D) – A process in which a cell inhibits its neighboring cells from adopting the same fate, playing a role in cell differentiation rather than expanding the stem cell pool.

explanation.text: Erythropoiesis: Since hemoglobin is not present in BFU-E, it can not transport oxygen. (Option A) Multipotent hematopoietic stem cell gives rise to all the cells circulating in blood. (Option B)

questions.question: How many oxygen atoms can one molecule of hemoglobin bind?

explanation.text: Hemoglobin: Hb synthesis begins in the polychromatophil erythroblasts. The most common form of hemoglobin found in adults is HbA, which is a combination of 2 alpha chains and 2 beta chains. The heme group in one Hb molecule has 4 atoms of iron, which binds to 4 molecules of oxygen or 8 atoms of oxygen (option D) Therefore, each Hb molecule carries 4 oxygen molecules to the tissues.

questions.question: Which of the following is the primary protein responsible for binding and transporting free heme in the bloodstream?

explanation.text: Hemopexin is a primary protein that is responsible for binding and transporting free heme in the bloodstream. When RBC undergoes hemolysis, heme is released into the blood. Free heme is potentially toxic due to its ability to generate reactive oxygen species and cause oxidative damage. Hemopexin binds to free heme with high affinity, facilitating safe transport of the liver for degradation and prevention of toxicity (option D).

**Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin, but not free heme (Option A):** Albumin maintains osmotic pressure and serves as a carrier protein for various substances, including hormones, fatty acids, and drugs, but is not a carrier of heme (Option B) Transferrin is responsible for transfer of iron in the bloodstream. (Option C)

questions.question: Which of the following describes the chloride ion exchange in red blood cells, where bicarbonate ions are exchanged for chloride ions to maintain electrical neutrality?

explanation.text: The chloride shift, also known as the Hamburger effect, is the process by which bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) exits red blood cells (RBCs) in exchange for chloride (Cl⁻) ions, maintaining electrical neutrality.

Mechanism: In peripheral tissues, CO₂ diffuses into RBCs and reacts with water, catalysed by carbonic anhydrase, forming HCO₃⁻ and H⁺. HCO₃⁻ is transported out of the RBC into the plasma via the band 3 protein in exchange for Cl⁻. This shift maintains ionic balance and facilitates CO₂ transport in the blood. In the lungs, the process reverses, allowing CO₂ exhalation.

Chloride shift (Hamburger phenomenon) vs Reverse chloride shift: Feature Chloride shift Reverse chloride shift Location Tissues Lungs Process CO₂ enters RBCs, forming H⁺CO₂ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. HCO₃⁻ exits in exchange for Cl⁻ CO₂ exits RBCs.

HCO₃⁻ re-enters RBCs in exchange for Cl⁻ Effect on RBCs Chloride influx causes water influx, swelling RBCs Chloride efflux balances HCO₃⁻ re-entry, CO₂ is released Impact on haematocrit Increases hematocrit due to RBC swelling Primarily facilitates CO₂ release, indirectly affecting hematocrit Haldane Effect (Option A) is incorrect because it describes increased CO₂ binding to haemoglobin in deoxygenated blood, enhancing CO₂ transport.
**Root Effect (Option B):** Incorrect because it refers to a reduction in hemoglobin’s O₂ carrying capacity in acidic conditions.
**Bohr Effect (Option C):** is incorrect because it refers to the effect of CO₂ and H⁺ on oxygen affinity, where increased CO₂ lowers haemoglobin’s oxygen affinity, promoting O₂ unloading in tissues.

questions.question: Which of the following factors causes a rightward shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve?

explanation.text: A rightward shift in the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve means reduced oxygen affinity, facilitating oxygen unloading to tissues. This occurs in conditions where tissues require more oxygen, such as exercise or metabolic activity.

Factors causing a rightward shift (Bohr effect): ↑ CO₂: Increases carbonic acid (H⁺CO₂) formation, lowering pH and promoting oxygen release. ↑ H⁺ (↓ pH): Acidic conditions reduce haemoglobin's oxygen affinity. ↑ Temperature: Higher metabolic activity increases oxygen demand. ↑ 2,3-BPG (DPG): Enhances O₂ unloading by stabilising the deoxygenated form of haemoglobin.

Bohr Effect A shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right in response to increases in blood CO2 and H+ levels has a significant effect by enhancing the release of O2 from the blood in the tissues and enhancing oxygenation of the blood in the lungs Mechanism Increase in CO 2: CO 2 diffuses from tissues into the blood, forming carbonic acid (H⁺CO₂), dissociating into H+ and HCO 3 -. This increase in H+ lowers blood pH. Decrease in pH: Lower pH shifts the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve to the right, causing haemoglobin to release O2 more readily.

Effects in Tissues Higher CO2 and lower pH cause haemoglobin to release O2, delivering more O2 to metabolically active tissues. Effects in Lungs Expelling CO2 in the lungs decreases blood CO2 levels and increases pH, shifting the dissociation curve to the left and allowing haemoglobin to bind O2 more readily for transport.

Factors Influencing the Bohr Effect Increased CO2 concentration Increased blood temperature Increased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPG) concentration: BPG binds to haemoglobin, reducing its affinity for O2 and promoting O2 release.
**Increase in O₂ (Option B):** is incorrect because higher O₂ levels promote oxygen binding rather than a rightward shift.
**Decrease in CO₂ (Option C):** is incorrect because low CO₂ leads to higher pH, causing a leftward shift (increased O₂ affinity, reduced unloading).
**Decrease in Temperature (Option D):** is incorrect because low temperature stabilises haemoglobin’s oxygen-binding state, shifting the curve leftward.

explanation.text: Erythropoietin (EPO) is produced from peritubular epithelium cells of the kidney and perivenous hepatocytes of the liver. Incorrect Options: Option B, C & D are incorrect.

questions.question: What would be the duration for preserving red blood cells (RBCs) using Acid Citrate Dextrose (ACD) for storage, when phosphate is added alone and when adenine and phosphate are added together to ACD?

explanation.text: Red Blood Cells (RBCs) Preservation using ACD (Acid Citrate Dextrose): ACD is an anticoagulant solution used for the preservation of blood. When RBCs are preserved using ACD alone, the duration of storage is approximately 21 days. Addition of Adenine and Phosphate to ACD: Adenine and phosphate are often added to the ACD solution to enhance the preservation of RBCs.

With the addition of adenine and phosphate to ACD, the duration of storage is extended to approximately 35 days. These additives provide necessary nutrients and enhance the storage conditions, allowing for a longer preservation period of red blood cells.

questions.question: What is the blood group determined by the agglutination test depicted below?

explanation.text: O positive: In this case, there is no agglutination in either A or B antigens, indicating the absence of ABO antigens on the red blood cells. Blood group O is known as the universal donor because individuals with blood group O do not have A or B antigens on their red blood cells. Incorrect options: Option A: B positive: Since there is no agglutination in the B antigen, it is not indicative of blood group B. Therefore, option a) is incorrect.
Option B: A positive: Similarly, since there is no agglutination in the A antigen, it is not indicative of blood group A. Therefore, option b) is incorrect.

Option D: AB positive: Agglutination in both A and B antigens would indicate the presence of both A and B antigens on the red blood cells, which corresponds to blood group AB. However, since no agglutination is observed in the A or B antigens in this case, blood group AB is not the correct option. Therefore, option d) is incorrect.

questions.question: Which of the following is not synthesized by the liver?

explanation.text: Immunoglobulins, also known as antibodies, are primarily produced by plasma cells, which are a type of white blood cell derived from B lymphocytes. While the liver is involved in immune-related functions, such as phagocytosis by Kupffer cells, it does not synthesize immunoglobulins. Incorrect options Option A: Albumin is a protein synthesized by the liver.

It is the most abundant protein in the blood and plays a crucial role in maintaining oncotic pressure, transporting substances such as hormones and drugs, and regulating fluid balance. Option B: Coagulation factors, such as fibrinogen, prothrombin, and factors VII, VIII, IX, X, are produced by the liver. These factors are essential for blood clotting and are involved in the coagulation cascade.

Option C: Acute phase proteins, including C-reactive protein, haptoglobin, and serum amyloid A, are synthesized by the liver. They are part of the immune response and play a role in inflammation and tissue repair.

questions.question: cGMP is the second messenger of

explanation.text: Nitric oxide (NO) activates the enzyme guanylate cyclase, which converts guanosine triphosphate (GTP) into cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP). cGMP then serves as the second messenger, mediating various cellular responses. NO is a key signaling molecule involved in several physiological processes, including v asodilation, neurotransmission, and immune regulation.

Incorrect Options: Option A: Somatostatin - Somatostatin acts through G-protein-coupled receptors, but its second messenger system involves inhibitory G-proteins and intracellular pathways such as the inhibition of adenylate cyclase and decrease in cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels. It does not involve cGMP as the second messenger. Option B: Angiotensin II- This option is incorrect.

Angiotensin II primarily acts through the angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1 receptor) and utilizes the inositol trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG) signaling pathway, leading to an increase in intracellular calcium levels. It does not involve cGMP as the second messenger.

Option C: ADH (antidiuretic hormone, also known as vasopressin)- ADH acts through the V2 receptor and utilizes the cAMP signaling pathway, activating protein kinase A (PKA) and regulating water reabsorption in the kidneys. It does not involve cGMP as the second messenger.
